strengths: The paper identifies a useful empirical phenomenon: standard MOTR’s detection AP rises from 60.0 to 66.3 when track queries are removed, clearly motivating the study of detection–association interference.
SelfMOTR is conceptually simple and practically relevant: it reuses encoder features, generates internal box proposals in a detection-only decoder pass, and avoids an external detector at inference.

The core mechanism produces substantial gains on DanceTrack validation. Self proposals improve HOTA from 51.2 to 58.2, AssA from 38.4 to 47.4, and IDF1 from 49.1 to 59.0. The controlled comparison against learnable anchors with HSV augmentation and CrowdHuman training also favors self proposals by 3.8 HOTA.

The experimental section examines several prior-injection strategies, proposal sources, proposal thresholds, decoder depth, detection AP, and runtime. The final model is competitive on DanceTrack test, reaching 69.2 HOTA and the highest reported AssA among the listed end-to-end methods, while retaining 20.7 FPS.
The presentation is generally clear, and the paper appropriately acknowledges that the mechanism has only been instantiated in a MOTR-style architecture.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is not fully established. SelfMOTR adds a separately supervised detection pass, an additional proposal loss, and extra decoder computation; consequently, its gains do not by themselves show that reusing a pre-existing 'hidden detector' or resolving query competition is the decisive factor. Controls with an equally supervised dual-pass model using independent weights, detached proposals, or alternative proposal encodings would help isolate the claimed mechanism.

Generalization evidence is mixed. On MOT17 test, SelfMOTR obtains 57.5 HOTA, below the reported MOTR baseline of 57.8 and substantially below CO-MOT’s 60.1; DetA and MOTA also fall below MOTR. The improvement is confined mainly to association, so broad claims of stronger tracking or consistently higher performance are not supported across the two benchmarks.

The strongest DanceTrack result depends heavily on additional HSV augmentation and CrowdHuman training: self proposals alone reach 58.2 validation HOTA, whereas the combined data/augmentation stage reaches 64.3. Although Table 7 supplies a useful matched comparison, the paper does not clearly specify whether all test-set baselines use comparable extra data and augmentation, limiting the fairness of the state-of-the-art comparison.

Reproducibility is inadequate in several important respects. 'CAL supervision' is used but never defined or properly attributed; the final denoising stage is neither described in the method nor parameterized; HSV augmentation settings are absent; and the final proposal-pass depth, number of detection queries, loss weights, query-management details, and code availability are not reported clearly enough to reconstruct the model.

The empirical study reports no repeated runs, uncertainty, or sensitivity beyond two proposal thresholds. This matters particularly for small differences such as 69.2 versus 69.4 HOTA on DanceTrack and the 0.1–0.3 point changes attributed to denoising or self proposals relative to frozen proposals.

Evaluated as an Algorithms/General contribution because no contribution type is declared, the two-pass self-proposal construction is sensible but incremental relative to MOTRv2-style proposal injection and existing detection-only/query-management mechanisms. Given the mixed cross-dataset results and missing controls, the evidence presently supports a slight preference for rejection despite clear practical merit.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant detection-association interference in MOTR and supports it with a clear controlled inference comparison: removing track queries raises DanceTrack detection AP from 60.0 to 66.3.

The proposed self-proposal mechanism is simple and intuitive: a detection-only decoder pass supplies confidence-conditioned 4D anchors to a shared tracking pass, avoiding a separately pretrained external detector while reusing encoder features.
DanceTrack results are competitive. SelfMOTR reaches 69.2 HOTA and 72.5 IDF1, approximately matching CO-MOT, and obtains the strongest reported AssA among the listed end-to-end methods.

The paper includes useful studies of alternative prior-injection mechanisms, proposal source, confidence threshold, decoder depth, and runtime. Under the augmented controlled recipe, self proposals improve HOTA from 60.5 to 64.3 over learnable anchors, while inference remains relatively fast at 20.7 FPS.
weaknesses: The empirical case does not generalize convincingly. On MOT17, SelfMOTR obtains 57.5 HOTA, slightly below the paper's MOTR baseline of 57.8 and substantially below recent end-to-end methods around 60 HOTA. The only emphasized gain is AssA, while DetA, MOTA, and overall HOTA regress. This conflicts with the broad framing that the mechanism resolves a general MOTR detection-association problem.

The novelty is modest for an Algorithms/General contribution. The hidden detection capability is explicitly presented as an observation already reported by CO-MOT, and the final method largely consists of running a supervised detection pass and feeding its boxes as anchors into a second pass. Its distinction from MOTRv2-style detector proposals and CO-MOT-style auxiliary queries is one of proposal provenance and weight sharing rather than a substantially new tracking formulation.

The headline improvement over the basic MOTR baseline is confounded by several recipe changes. Table 5 adds HSV augmentation, CrowdHuman training, QIMv2, and denoising alongside the proposed mechanism. Table 7 gives the more relevant controlled comparison, where the gain over learnable anchors is 3.8 HOTA rather than the much larger improvement suggested by the main cumulative ablation. Comparable controlled baselines for stronger contemporary architectures are absent.

Important implementation details needed for reproduction are missing or unclear, including the number and handling of detection queries/proposals, whether proposal boxes and confidence scores are detached between passes, treatment of unmatched predictions in Eq. 1, exact HSV augmentation, and the denoising procedure that appears only in the experiments. The roles of CAL and QIMv2 are also not made self-contained.

Table 9 does not fully establish the claimed removal of detection-association conflict. The detection-only proposal branch necessarily excludes track queries, while the other measurement comes after proposals have already been injected into a different tracking computation. Thus, the 0.3 AP gap is not a clean counterpart to the original MOTR intervention and cannot by itself demonstrate that interference has been eliminated.

The evaluation is limited to two pedestrian-tracking datasets, with success concentrated on DanceTrack. There are no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, qualitative failure analysis, robustness tests under occlusion or proposal errors, or experiments showing portability to the stronger architectures named in the limitations.

Calling the method fully end-to-end and detector-free needs qualification: it contains an explicit, directly supervised detection stage and a hard confidence-threshold selection operation. It avoids an external detector and is jointly trained, which is valuable, but the current terminology overstates the conceptual difference from a two-stage detection-proposal pipeline.

Overall, the strong DanceTrack result and efficient design provide real merit, but limited originality, incomplete methodological specification, confounded comparisons, and failure to improve overall MOT17 tracking leave the scientific case slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful empirical phenomenon: standard MOTR’s detection AP rises from 60.0 to 66.3 when track queries are removed. This provides concrete evidence of detection–association interference and motivates the method well.

SelfMOTR is a simple and practically relevant Algorithms/General contribution: it converts predictions from a shared-weight detection-only pass into proposals for the tracking pass, avoiding the separately pretrained detector used by approaches such as MOTRv2.
The DanceTrack results are strong. SelfMOTR obtains 69.2 HOTA and 72.5 IDF1, competitive with CO-MOT, while attaining the best AssA (59.3) among the reported end-to-end methods.

The ablations are unusually broad and generally support the design. Self proposals improve the matched MOTR baseline from 51.2 to 58.2 HOTA; proposal-source comparisons show that internal proposals match pretrained-detector proposals; and detection AP drops only 0.3 points when track queries are introduced, versus 6.3 for MOTR.

The paper studies several alternative ways of exploiting detection priors—full detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, and anchor proposals—providing insight beyond the final architecture.
Efficiency is considered explicitly. Reusing encoder features limits the two-pass overhead: the reported speed decreases from 24.8 to 20.7 FPS while accuracy improves substantially.
The manuscript is clear, well organized, appropriately situated relative to MOTR-style trackers, and candidly acknowledges that evaluation is limited to the MOTR architecture family.
weaknesses: Evidence of generalization is mixed. On MOT17, SelfMOTR reaches only 57.5 HOTA, below the reported MOTR baseline (57.8) and substantially below CO-MOT (60.1) and MOTRv3 (60.2); it improves AssA only modestly while reducing DetA and MOTA. Thus the central benefit is demonstrated convincingly mainly on DanceTrack.

The novelty is moderate: the principal mechanism is an extra detection-only decoder pass followed by proposal-conditioned tracking. Since proposal-based MOTR variants already exist, the advance rests primarily on generating proposals internally with shared weights rather than on a fundamentally new tracking formulation.

Some gains in the cumulative ablation are confounded by training changes. HSV augmentation and CrowdHuman training are introduced together and account for 6.1 HOTA, whereas the final denoising stage is barely beneficial. Although Table 7 gives matched comparisons, isolating HSV from additional data and reporting the final test configuration more transparently would strengthen attribution.

Important implementation details needed for reproduction are underspecified, including the final proposal-pass decoder depth, number and initialization of detection queries, exact denoising procedure, whether proposal boxes or scores are detached between passes, and the complete query filtering/duplicate-handling procedure. The confidence threshold appears inferable as 0.05 but is not explicitly identified as the final setting.

The evaluation reports single runs without variance or seed analysis. Several close comparisons—69.2 versus 69.4 HOTA on DanceTrack and 58.0 versus 58.2 in the proposal-source ablation—therefore should not be interpreted as meaningful differences.

The claim of being “fully end-to-end” needs qualification because confidence thresholding and variable proposal selection are discrete operations. Joint optimization of the shared network is plausible, but the manuscript should explicitly explain gradient flow through proposal construction.

The analysis is restricted to two pedestrian-tracking datasets and one architectural family. Testing the mechanism on a stronger query-based baseline, or at least on an additional domain, would better establish that the observed hidden-detector phenomenon is general rather than MOTR/DanceTrack-specific.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important limitation of joint detection-association decoding and proposes a simple, self-contained remedy: a detection-only pass generates spatial proposals that are consumed by a second tracking pass while sharing the encoder and decoder parameters.

The central controlled result is substantial: on DanceTrack validation, adding self-proposals improves the authors' MOTR baseline from 51.2 to 58.2 HOTA, with large gains in AssA (38.4 to 47.4) and IDF1 (49.1 to 59.0). The proposal-source ablation further shows that internal proposals match or slightly exceed proposals from a separately pretrained MOTR detector.

Evaluation covers several distinct regimes. SelfMOTR is competitive with leading end-to-end methods on DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA), performs strongly on BFT (71.1 HOTA), and provides results on AnimalTrack and MOT17, including a candid discussion of its weaker MOT17 performance.

The study of alternative prior-injection mechanisms, proposal thresholds, decoder depth, data scaling, detection AP, and runtime provides useful empirical insight beyond the headline benchmark results. The reported 20.7 FPS versus 24.8 FPS for the baseline suggests a moderate practical overhead.
The method is clearly motivated and generally well presented. It avoids an external detector at inference and could be straightforwardly useful to researchers building query-propagation trackers.
weaknesses: The mechanistic explanation based on Track Attention Mass is correlational. The paper labels intermediate mass and high entropy as a 'healthy' regime, but does not causally intervene on attention or show that these statistics predict discovery errors, duplicate detections, or performance across queries and frames. Thus, the results establish the benefit of proposal conditioning more convincingly than the claimed attention-based mechanism.

The strongest final configuration is not isolated cleanly against a matched strong baseline. Table 6 shows that self-proposals contribute +7.0 HOTA, while HSV augmentation and CrowdHuman training contribute another +6.1, but there is no fully matched comparison applying the complete recipe to the strongest alternative, such as CO-MOT or a modern anchor-query MOTR baseline. The authors' reimplemented MOTR validation baseline is also below the published MOTR test result, complicating attribution of the final competitive performance.

Important implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing or ambiguous: the number of detection queries, whether proposal boxes and confidence embeddings are detached between passes, how gradients behave through hard confidence filtering, the precise handling of unmatched predictions in Eq. 3, and the detection-pass depth used for the headline models. The project-page field is blank and no code or release commitment is provided.

Calling the method fully end-to-end requires qualification because proposal selection uses a hard confidence threshold between two passes. The model is jointly trained and detector-free, but the manuscript should clarify the differentiability boundary and distinguish these properties.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. The AnimalTrack advantage over TransTrack is only 0.1 HOTA, no multiple-seed variability is reported, and SelfMOTR remains clearly behind leading end-to-end methods on MOT17 (57.5/58.4 versus about 60.1-60.2 HOTA). The claim that the detection-association conflict is 'practically removed' also rests on one AP comparison and does not establish generality beyond this architecture.

The efficiency analysis reports FPS on one GPU but omits FLOPs, memory, parameter counts, and matched measurements for different proposal-pass depths. Since the main design invokes the decoder twice, these measurements are important for substantiating the description as lightweight.

There are minor presentation and attribution issues, including an incorrect DanceTrack citation attached to the AnimalTrack dataset description and insufficient reporting of sample counts or uncertainty for the attention distributions. These are repairable but weaken polish.

strengths: The manuscript identifies a practically relevant weakness of joint detection-association decoding and proposes a simple two-pass solution: the same model first generates spatial proposals without track queries and then combines these proposals with propagated tracks. The proposal mechanism produces substantial improvements over the reported MOTR baseline on DanceTrack validation: self proposals raise HOTA from 51.2 to 58.2, AssA from 38.4 to 47.4, and IDF1 from 49.1 to 59.0. The comparison among learned anchors, frozen-detector anchors, and internal proposals is useful evidence that internally generated proposals can replace an auxiliary detector.

Evaluation spans DanceTrack, BFT, AnimalTrack, and MOT17. SelfMOTR is competitive with strong end-to-end trackers on DanceTrack, and the BFT result is particularly encouraging. The paper also reports detection, association, identity, accuracy, and runtime metrics rather than relying on one headline number.
The paper is generally readable, and the candid MOT17 appendix usefully exposes a setting in which the method does not improve over established end-to-end systems.
weaknesses: The work is best assessed as an Algorithms/General submission because no contribution type is declared. Its algorithmic novelty is limited: it effectively runs an internal detector pass followed by a tracking pass with shared parameters. The distinction from a detect-then-track design is therefore partly semantic, and the paper does not establish that parameter sharing or confidence-conditioned query construction constitutes a sufficiently original architectural contribution.

The strongest causal claim—that track-query attention causes suppressed detection—is not convincingly demonstrated. Track Attention Mass is descriptive, attention weights are not causal explanations, and the paper provides no intervention, per-error correlation, or controlled manipulation of attention. The designation of mass near 0.4 and high entropy as a “healthy” regime is asserted rather than validated; aggregation across heads, frames, and samples is also insufficiently specified.

The main gains are confounded by unequal training recipes. Table 6 shows large improvements from HSV augmentation and CrowdHuman training, while denoising contributes little. Although Table 4b includes a stronger anchor baseline, the paper does not provide the fully controlled test-set comparison needed to isolate self proposals while matching initialization, data, augmentation, QIMv2, denoising, training budget, and tuning effort. Consequently, the headline improvement over standard MOTR overstates evidence attributable solely to the proposed mechanism.

Evidence against the strongest contemporary alternatives is modest. On DanceTrack, SelfMOTR is slightly below CO-MOT in HOTA (69.2 versus 69.4), and on AnimalTrack it improves over TransTrack by only 0.1 HOTA while remaining below the non-end-to-end QDTrack result. The 1.5-HOTA BFT gain is promising, but no repeated runs, variance estimates, or significance analysis are reported.

Several implementation details necessary for reproduction are missing: whether gradients from the tracking pass flow through predicted anchors and confidence filtering; treatment of unmatched predictions in Eq. 3; proposal counts and duplicate handling; precise decoder depth used in final models; loss coefficients other than λprop; and ablations for confidence encoding, the ten learned fallback anchors, parameter sharing, and λprop. Only two proposal thresholds are evaluated.

Figure 6 reports performance across decoder depths on both validation and test sets. Using test performance to analyze or select architectural depth risks test-set tuning, and the manuscript does not clarify whether the final configuration was fixed before these evaluations. Similar diagnostic analysis is performed on the BFT and AnimalTrack test sets.

The efficiency case is incomplete. A second decoder pass reduces throughput from 24.8 to 20.7 FPS, but the paper omits FLOPs, memory, latency by decoder depth, hardware-normalized comparisons with leading methods, and training-cost overhead. Calling the design computationally efficient is therefore only weakly supported.

There is no qualitative tracking analysis, failure taxonomy, or study of proposal errors under occlusion, crowding, and domain shift. Given the poor MOT17 results and dependence on confident current-frame proposals, such evidence is important for understanding when the approach succeeds or fails. Overall, the method has merit, but limited novelty, confounded comparisons, and an overinterpreted attention diagnostic leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper presents a simple and practically meaningful idea: generate spatial proposals through a detection-only pass of the tracker itself, then combine them with propagated track queries in a shared tracking pass. This avoids a separately trained external detector while directly addressing detection–association interference.

The empirical improvements over the matched MOTR baseline are substantial. On DanceTrack validation, self proposals improve HOTA from 51.2 to 58.2, AssA from 38.4 to 47.4, and IDF1 from 49.1 to 59.0. The proposal-source ablation further shows that internal proposals perform comparably to anchors from a separately pretrained detector.

Evaluation covers four challenging benchmarks. SelfMOTR is competitive with the strongest end-to-end methods on DanceTrack, obtains the best reported BFT results in the comparison, and remains competitive on AnimalTrack. Reporting the weaker MOT17 outcome is commendably transparent and helps delimit where the method is effective.

The paper provides useful diagnostic and ablation evidence beyond headline benchmark numbers, including detection with and without track queries, alternative prior-injection mechanisms, proposal thresholds, decoder depth, data scaling, runtime, and successive components.

The method retains practical online speed: 20.7 FPS on an L40S versus 24.8 FPS for the anchor-based baseline, because the backbone and encoder are evaluated only once. The presentation is generally clear, and the architecture is easy to understand.
weaknesses: The attention analysis is correlational and does not establish the proposed causal explanation. Balanced Track Attention Mass and high entropy are interpreted as a 'healthy' regime without showing that these statistics predict detection failures or that directly manipulating them changes performance. Aggregation over heads, frames, objects, and sequences is also insufficiently specified, with no uncertainty or sample counts.

Important implementation details needed for reproduction are missing or ambiguous: the backbone variant, default number of layers in the proposal pass, number of detection queries, gradient flow or detachment through selected boxes and confidence scores, handling of the non-differentiable threshold, and matching/query-management behavior when proposal and propagated track queries overlap. The project-page field is empty, and no code or repeated-run statistics are provided.

The final DanceTrack result combines self proposals with CrowdHuman training, HSV augmentation, QIMv2, and denoising. The cumulative ablation usefully separates these factors on validation, but there is no equally controlled test-set comparison against a baseline using precisely the same training recipe. Consequently, the complete 69.2-HOTA result cannot be attributed solely to SelfMOTR.

Some claims are overstated. AnimalTrack is trained on the target dataset, so the statement that the formulation 'transfers' or demonstrates generalization beyond the training regime is unsupported. Its 45.5 HOTA is only 0.1 above TransTrack and below the non-end-to-end QDTrack result. Likewise, 'fully end-to-end' should be qualified because the system uses two decoder passes and explicit confidence-thresholded proposal selection, even though it is detector-free in the important sense of requiring no separate detector.

Efficiency evidence is limited to FPS on one GPU. FLOPs, memory, latency as target count changes, and accuracy–speed measurements for the proposed shallow-pass configurations are absent. The claim that practitioners can reduce the proposal pass to one or two layers would be stronger with corresponding measured FPS values.

The method is conceptually incremental—largely replacing externally generated anchor proposals with predictions from a shared detection pass—and the strongest improvement over detector-generated anchors is small (58.0 to 58.2 HOTA). Its value therefore rests mainly on simplicity and eliminating the external model rather than a fundamentally new tracking mechanism.
